topics.title: Numbers to 1000
topics.intro: Every 3-digit number is built from hundreds, tens and ones. 572 is 5 hundreds, 7 tens and 2 ones, and it can be split in other ways too: 400 + 170 + 2.
topics.teach: Explain what happens to 395 when you add 10.
topics.talk: Read the numbers on car number plates or house doors and ask {him} what each digit is worth.

visual.caption: 5 hundreds, 7 tens and 2 ones make 572. It can also be split as 400 + 170 + 2.

topics.title: Adding and subtracting in your head
topics.intro: Adding 1s, 10s or 100s to a 3-digit number changes one digit, unless it crosses a boundary. For 99, add 100 and take 1 away!
topics.teach: Explain a quick way to work out 456 + 99.
topics.talk: In the car, ask {him} for 10 more, 100 more, then 1 less than a number.

topics.title: Column addition and subtraction
topics.intro: Line the digits up in columns: hundreds, tens, ones. Start with the ones. When a column is too big (or too small), exchange with the next column.
topics.teach: Explain how you would check 532 − 278 using addition.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to estimate first, then work it out, then check.

head: H
T
O
visual.caption: 543 − 278. 3 − 8 won’t go: exchange a ten, so 13 − 8 = 5. 3 − 7 won’t go: exchange a hundred, so 13 − 7 = 6. Then 4 − 2 = 2.

topics.title: The 3, 4 and 8 times tables
topics.intro: The 4 times table is double the 2s, and the 8 times table is double the 4s. If you know 3 × 4 = 12, you also know 30 × 4 = 120!
topics.teach: Explain how 3 × 8 = 24 helps you work out 30 × 8.
topics.talk: Quick-fire 8 times table on the way to school.

visual.caption: Eight 3s are double four 3s: 4 × 3 = 12, so 8 × 3 = 24.

topics.title: Multiplying 2-digit numbers
topics.intro: To multiply 34 × 3, split 34 into 30 and 4. Multiply each part, then add: 90 + 12 = 102. A grid helps you keep track.
topics.teach: Explain how to work out 26 × 4 with a grid.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how many wheels on 23 cars.

topics.title: Dividing and remainders
topics.intro: Dividing shares into equal groups. Sometimes there are some left over: the remainder. In stories, think carefully about what to do with it!
topics.teach: Explain why 26 children need 7 tables of 4, not 6.
topics.talk: Share some sweets or grapes equally and talk about the remainder.

visual.caption: 17 sweets shared into 5 bags: 3 in each bag and 2 left over. 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2.

topics.title: Fractions of amounts and tenths
topics.intro: To find a fraction of an amount, divide by the bottom number and multiply by the top. Tenths come from sharing something into 10 equal parts.
topics.teach: Explain how to find {{3/4}} of 20.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {{1/4}} of an hour is in minutes.

visual.caption: {{3/4}} of 24: share 24 into 4 equal parts of 6. Three parts make 18.
One whole shared into 10 equal parts: each part is one tenth. 3 tenths are shaded.

topics.title: Equivalent fractions, adding and comparing
topics.intro: Fractions that look different can be equal: {{1/2}} = {{2/4}} = {{4/8}}. When the bottom numbers are the same, just add or take away the top numbers.
topics.teach: Explain why {{1/3}} is bigger than {{1/5}}.
topics.talk: Fold paper into halves, quarters and eighths and compare.

visual.caption: {{1/2}} = {{2/4}} = {{4/8}}: the shaded parts are the same length.

topics.title: Length, mass and capacity
topics.intro: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 g = 1 kg and 1000 ml = 1 l. Change measures into the same unit before you compare or add them.
topics.teach: Explain how to change 2 m 35 cm into centimetres.
topics.talk: Weigh ingredients together when baking.

topics.title: Money and change
topics.intro: £1 = 100p, so £3.45 is 345p. To find change, count on from the price to the money you paid.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the change from £5 for something costing £3.70.
topics.talk: Let {him} work out the change at the shop before the cashier does.

topics.title: Time to the minute and the 24-hour clock
topics.intro: Read the long hand to the exact minute by counting in 5s, then 1s. a.m. is before midday, p.m. is after. 24-hour clocks carry on after 12: 3 p.m. is 15:00.
topics.teach: Explain how to change 4:30 p.m. into 24-hour time.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to read train or cinema times in 24-hour clock.

head: 12-hour clock
24-hour clock
visual.caption: For p.m. times from 1 p.m., add 12 to the hour: 3 p.m. is 15:00. (12:30 p.m. stays 12:30.)

topics.title: Angles, turns and lines
topics.intro: A right angle is a quarter turn, like the corner of a book. Other angles are bigger or smaller. Lines can be horizontal, vertical, parallel (never meet) or perpendicular (meet at a right angle).
topics.teach: Explain how many right angles are in a full turn.
topics.talk: Hunt for right angles, parallel lines and perpendicular lines around the house.

topics.title: Bar charts, pictograms and tables
topics.intro: Read the scale carefully: it might go up in 2s, 5s or 10s, and a bar can stop halfway between lines. In a pictogram, check the key.
topics.teach: Explain how to read a bar that stops halfway between 20 and 30.
topics.talk: Make a bar chart of the family’s favourite planets.

topics.title: Two-step problems
topics.intro: Some problems need two steps. Work out what you need to know first, do that, then use the answer for the second step.
topics.teach: Explain the two steps in a problem about buying tickets and getting change.
topics.talk: Make up a two-step superhero problem for each other.

topics.title: 2D and 3D shapes
topics.intro: Year 3 shape facts: prisms, pyramids, faces, edges and vertices, and the special names for lines.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a prism and a pyramid.
topics.talk: Find a prism and a pyramid in the kitchen or at the shops.

visual.caption: A triangular prism: 2 triangle ends and 3 rectangle sides. 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.
A square-based pyramid: 1 square base and 4 triangles. 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices.

topics.title: Year 3 facts to know
topics.intro: Facts worth knowing by heart: Roman numerals on clocks, seconds in a minute, days in each month, and more.
topics.teach: Explain how to remember which months have 30 days.
topics.talk: Find Roman numerals on a clock face and read them together.

topics.title: Thinking hard: Year 3 puzzles
topics.intro: Greater depth means explaining, proving and spotting patterns. Take your time, try examples, and look for the trick.
topics.teach: Explain how you know your answer must be right.
topics.talk: Ask {him} one puzzle at dinner and let {him} explain {her} thinking.

topics.title: Times tables to 12 × 12
topics.intro: Year 4 learns every table up to 12 × 12. Use tricks: 6s are double 3s, 9s are 10s take away one lot, 12s are 10s plus 2s.
topics.teach: Explain the trick for the 9 times table.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for 7 × 8 at breakfast every day for a week.

visual.caption: Find 7 × 9: go along to 7 and down to 9. The answer is 63.

topics.title: Negative numbers
topics.intro: Numbers below zero are negative, like −3°C on a cold night (or on Mars!). Count back through zero: 2, 1, 0, −1, −2.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between −5°C and 3°C.
topics.talk: Look at the freezer or weather forecast for temperatures below zero.

topics.title: Tenths and hundredths as decimals
topics.intro: A decimal point separates whole numbers from parts. 0.3 means 3 tenths; 0.25 means 25 hundredths. Racing times use them: 1.25 seconds!
topics.teach: Explain why 0.5 is the same as {{1/2}}.
topics.talk: Look at prices or race times with decimal points together.

visual.caption: 25 of the 100 squares are shaded: 2 whole columns (2 tenths) and 5 more squares (5 hundredths).
25 hundredths is written 0.25.

topics.title: Area
topics.intro: Area is the space inside a shape, measured in squares. For a rectangle, multiply the length by the width.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between area and perimeter.
topics.talk: Count the tiles on a floor or wall and work out the area.

topics.title: Rounding
topics.intro: Rounding gives a friendly number that is close: 487 rounds to 490 (nearest 10) or 500 (nearest 100). Exactly halfway rounds up.
topics.teach: Explain how to round 650 to the nearest 100.
topics.talk: Round the prices in a shop to the nearest pound.

visual.caption: 487 is past the halfway point (485), so it is nearer to 490. 487 rounds to 490.

items.prompt: How many faces does a triangular prism have?
items.explain: Two triangle ends and three rectangle sides: 5 faces.

visual.caption: A triangular prism: 2 triangle ends and 3 rectangle sides. 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.

items.prompt: How many faces does a square-based pyramid have?
items.explain: One square base and four triangles meeting at the top.

visual.caption: A square-based pyramid: 1 square base and 4 triangles. 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices.

items.prompt: How many edges does a square-based pyramid have?
items.explain: 4 round the base and 4 going up to the point.

visual.caption: A square-based pyramid: 1 square base and 4 triangles. 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices.

items.prompt: How many vertices does a cuboid have?
items.explain: Like a cube: 4 on top and 4 underneath.

visual.caption: A cuboid: 4 vertices on top and 4 underneath. 8 vertices.

items.prompt: A 3D shape with the same shape all the way through, like a Toblerone box, is called a…
items.explain: Prisms have two matching end faces joined by rectangles.

visual.caption: A triangular prism: 2 triangle ends and 3 rectangle sides. 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.

items.prompt: Two lines that never meet, like train tracks, are called…
items.explain: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart for ever.

items.prompt: Two lines that meet at a right angle are called…
items.explain: The corner of a page has perpendicular edges.

items.prompt: A line that goes straight across, like the horizon, is…
items.explain: Horizontal lines go across; vertical lines go straight up and down.

items.prompt: A line that goes straight up and down, like a flagpole, is…
items.explain: Vertical lines point straight up.

items.prompt: How many sides does a heptagon have?
items.explain: Hepta means seven. A 50p coin is a heptagon with curved sides.

visual.caption: A heptagon has 7 sides.

items.prompt: What is a shape with 4 sides called?
items.explain: Squares, rectangles, kites and parallelograms are all quadrilaterals.

items.prompt: Which 2D shape has one curved edge and no corners?
items.explain: A circle has one curved edge. A semicircle has a curved edge AND a straight one.

items.prompt: What number is XII in Roman numerals?
items.explain: X = 10 and II = 2: XII = 12, at the top of many clocks.

items.prompt: What number is IX in Roman numerals?
items.explain: I before X means one less than ten: 9.

items.prompt: What number is IV in Roman numerals?
items.explain: I before V means one less than five: 4.

items.prompt: How many seconds are in 1 minute?
items.explain: The second hand goes round once every minute.

items.prompt: How many minutes are in 2 hours?
How many days are in a leap year?
items.explain: A leap year has an extra day: 29 February.

items.prompt: How many days are in April?
items.explain: “Thirty days has September, April, June and November…”

items.prompt: How many days are in December?
items.explain: All the months not in the rhyme (except February) have 31 days.

items.prompt: How many millimetres are in 1 centimetre?
items.explain: Look at a ruler: 10 tiny marks in every centimetre.

items.prompt: How many grams are in half a kilogram?
items.explain: Half of 1000 g is 500 g.

items.prompt: How many millilitres are in a quarter of a litre?
items.explain: A quarter of 1000 ml is 250 ml.

items.prompt: What is 24-hour time for midday?
items.explain: Midday is 12:00; midnight is 00:00.

items.prompt: What is the smallest 3-digit number?
items.explain: 99 is the biggest 2-digit number, and one more is 100.

items.prompt: What is the largest 3-digit number?
items.explain: 999: one more makes 1000, which has 4 digits.

items.prompt: Every number in the 8 times table is even. Always, sometimes or never true?

options.feedback: Try lots: 8, 16, 24, 32… every one is even.
8 itself is even!

items.explain: 8 is double 4, so every multiple of 8 is a double: always even.

items.prompt: Numbers in the 3 times table are odd. Always, sometimes or never true?

options.feedback: 6 is in the 3 times table and it is even.
3, 9 and 15 are odd and in the 3 times table.

items.explain: They go odd, even, odd, even: 3, 6, 9, 12…

items.prompt: Turbo works out 452 − 127 and gets 335. What went wrong?

options.text: He should have added: it is 579
options.feedback: It is a subtraction; the mistake is in the ones column.

items.explain: In the ones, 2 − 7 won’t go, so exchange a ten: 12 − 7 = 5, then 4 − 2 = 2 tens, 4 − 1 = 3 hundreds. 325.

head: H
T
O
visual.caption: 2 − 7 won’t go, so exchange a ten: 12 − 7 = 5. Now there are only 4 tens: 4 − 2 = 2. 452 − 127 = 325.

items.prompt: Using the digits 3, 6 and 9 once each, how many different 3-digit numbers can you make?

options.feedback: Each digit can go first, then there are two ways to arrange the other two: 3 × 2 = 6.
List them systematically: 369, 396, 639, 693, 936, 963.

items.explain: Work systematically: 369, 396, 639, 693, 936, 963. Six numbers.

items.prompt: {hero} says 298 + 405 = 1003. How can you tell straight away it is wrong?

options.feedback: They can! The estimate is the quick check.

options.text: You can’t tell without working it out
options.feedback: Estimating tells you quickly: about 700.

items.explain: Round first: 300 + 400 = 700. The real answer is 703.

items.prompt: When you divide a number by 4, can the remainder be 5?

options.feedback: With 5 left over you could share one more each.
The remainder is always less than 4 when you divide by 4.

items.explain: A remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by.

items.prompt: Rosa ate {{1/2}} of a small pizza. Blaze ate {{1/4}} of a huge pizza. Who ate more?

options.text: We can’t tell without knowing the size of each pizza
Rosa, because a half is more than a quarter
options.feedback: A half of something small can be less than a quarter of something huge.
It depends on the sizes.

items.explain: Fractions compare fairly only when the wholes are the same size. Great mathematicians spot that!

items.prompt: Which is NOT the same as 4 × 6?

options.feedback: 8 × 3 = 24, the same as 4 × 6.

items.explain: 4 × 6 = 24 = 8 × 3 = 2 × 12 (double one number, halve the other). But 4 + 6 = 10.

items.prompt: 7, 15, 23, 31… Will 100 be in this pattern?

options.text: No: every number in it is odd
Yes, if you keep on going
options.feedback: Adding 8 to an odd number always gives odd, and 100 is even.
Every number in the pattern is odd, so 100 never appears.

items.explain: 7 is odd, and adding 8 (even) keeps it odd for ever.
40 × 3 = 120, and 60 × 2 = 120. Both sides of = must be the same.

items.prompt: Captain Nova says “Half past 3 in the afternoon is 03:30.” Is she right?

options.feedback: 03:30 is half past 3 in the middle of the night!

items.explain: For p.m. times, add 12 to the hour: 3 + 12 = 15, so 15:30.

items.prompt: A square has 4 right angles. Can a triangle have 2 right angles?

options.text: No: its sides could never meet

options.feedback: Try drawing it: the two lines go straight up side by side and never join.
Size doesn’t matter: two right angles means the sides can’t meet.

items.explain: Two right angles at the ends of one side make two parallel lines, so no third corner can form.
